description:
FILED s464aw while writing #987's inverse-guard rows (that is how it was
found: the `do` boundary row failed for a reason that had nothing to do with
#987).  PRE-EXISTING -- identical on an 80b715c worktree.

`do { $x }` yields the VARIABLE in perl -- a do block is not a frame and does
not copy -- so an aliasing consumer writes through it.  PCL aliases only for a
PACKAGE variable; every LEXICAL kind loses it:

    our $g = 1;  for (do { $g }) { $_ = 5 }             perl 5   PCL 5   ok
    my  $f = 1;  for (do { $f }) { $_ = 5 }             perl 5   PCL 1   <-
    { my $b = 1; for (do { $b }) { $_ = 5 } }           perl 5   PCL 1   <-
    sub s2 { my $s = 1; for (do { $s }) { $_ = 5 } $s } perl 5   PCL 1   <-
    my  $f3 = 1; my $r = \do { $f3 }; $$r = 5;          perl 5   PCL 1   <-
    my  $f2 = 1; for ($f2) { $_ = 5 }                   perl 5   PCL 5   ok
                                                        (no `do': the bare
                                                         foreach DOES alias)

So the last row is the discriminator: the aliasing machinery works on a file
lexical, and it is the `do { }` lowering that drops it -- the block's value
arrives as the lexical's VALUE, not its cell.  A package variable survives
because its read goes through a different path (a symbol-macro / global cell)
that yields the box either way.

SILENT WRONG, and it is in the same family as #964/#987 but the OPPOSITE
direction: those two were PCL aliasing where perl copies; this is PCL copying
(or rather, never aliasing) where perl does not.

WHY IT IS NOT #987's: #987 is "an eval IS a frame".  `do { }` is the boundary
that proves the rule and #987's guard rows use `our` for exactly this reason,
with a comment saying so.  Fixing this one is about how a `do` block's value
leaves the block, not about frames at all.

SUSPECT (the cheap discriminating measurement, not yet taken): read the
emitted CL for `my $f = 1; my $r = \do { $f };` and for the `our` twin -- one
`./pl2cl` shows whether the do-block lowering wraps its value (a p-scalar-ctx
or an unbox) that the package-variable path does not reach.

BAR: the six rows above vs perl on both emission paths; corpus-diff if the fix
is in `Pl/` (likely) or the sweep if it is in `cl/`; a guard row beside
Pl/t/return-copy-01.t's E group, which already documents the boundary.
subject: do { $lexical } does not alias -- perl writes through a do block, PCL only does for a package variable
